newsitem.title: UK: ATHLETICS-IOC TO INTRODUCE TEST FOR TESTOSTERONE THIS YEAR.
newsitem.headline: ATHLETICS-IOC TO INTRODUCE TEST FOR TESTOSTERONE THIS YEAR.

text.p: The International Olympic Committee (IOC) will shortly introduce a test which can detect if an woman athlete has taken the male sex hormone testosterone.

At present athletes are suspended if their urine sample shows an excessively high ratio of testosterone to epitestosterone. But the present method does not show if the testosterone has been introduced artificially.
International Amateur Athletic Federation (IAAF) spokesman Giorgio Reineri told Reuters on Monday the new test would show definitely if an athlete had taken testosterone.
"I spoke yesterday to the head of the IOC medical commission Prince Alexandre de Merode," Reineri said from the IAAF's headquarters in Monte Carlo.
"He told me that in the next two or three months a test would be ready able to show if somebody had taken testosterone."
Reineri said the test could be ready in time for the world athletics championships in Athens in August.
U.S. athletics sources said at the weekend that American 400 metres hurdler Sandra Farmer-Patrick had been suspended for four years after testing positive for testosterone.
The sources said Farmer-Patrick, the world silver medallist at Stuttgart in 1993, had tested positive after the U.S. trials last year.

The American governing body U.S.A. Track and Field does not automatically suspend athletes after the first sample and Farmer-Patrick was allowed to compete at the Atlanta Olympics where she was eliminated in the semifinals.
The sources said she had subsequently been suspended after further tests were also positive.

Veteran Mary Slaney, a double gold medallist at the inaugural world championships in Helsinki 14 years ago, is also being investigated by the U.S. authorities over a drugs test at the American trials.

Slaney's lawyer Doriane Lambelet Coleman confirmed last week that a sample had shown a ratio higher than six-to-one, the level at which an athlete faces suspension, but added: "There has not been a suspension and we do not expect her to be suspended."

British middle-distance runner Diane Modahl, whose ratio was 42-1 in a test in Lisbon in 1994, successfully appealed against a four-year ban when she argued that the sample had been degraded after it had been stored in excessively hot conditions.
